finding: Guard-move verified sound: async_stream::stream! builds the async move generator eagerly, so the captured guard is dropped when an unpolled stream future is dropped; guard is constructed only after register() returns Ok, with no intervening ? or await

Cap-check ORDER was silently swapped (global-first -> per-user-first), so a globally saturated deployment reports SYNC_USER_LIMIT instead of SYNC_GLOBAL_LIMIT, masking a capacity incident as a per-account problem. Confirmed by 3 independent angles

The expires_at deadline signal frees the ACCOUNTING slot of a connection whose stream future, channel, tokio task and socket are all still alive - in exactly the black-holed-peer case it targets, the stream is not being polled (which is WHY it outlived its deadline), so nothing tears it down. The cap then bounds bookkeeping instead of real resources, letting a client accumulate server-side connections past the cap: a fail-closed DoS bound traded for unbounded growth

Doc claim 'two independent liveness signals, neither of which can false-positive a healthy stream' is FALSE: the deadline arm cannot fire while the generator is suspended at yield (backpressured client) or inside the periodic re-check's DB await, so a healthy-but-late stream is exactly what gets reaped

Self-contradictory doc: 'derived from the connection, not a tunable, so there is no arbitrary TTL to configure and no risk of reaping a healthy idle stream' describes DEADLINE_SLACK, which IS an arbitrary hardcoded 60s TTL, and the change's own test name says '...even_if_alive'

The outer repo's actual production change (the ConnGuard hoist in the chat handler) had NO test exercising it: every red-before-fix test drove the framework sync handler. Reverting handler.rs alone left the whole chat suite green

the_cap_is_still_enforced_... doc claimed 'through the same real handler', 'bodies polled', 'per-surface pinned id' - none true; it never issued a request and built ClientConns by hand, a mocked stand-in presented as the real path
TestResolver mints a fresh uuid per request, so 'N=20 > PER_USER_MAX_CONNECTIONS (12)' was meaningless and the per-iteration 200 assertion was vacuous (only the global cap of 512 could ever trip)
count_available_slots is called immediately after dropping a response with no wait or retry, but server-side reclamation is asynchronous - a timing race that will flake under load
The chat registry had no global-cap test at all, so the new global sweep branch in register() was entirely uncovered (the SDK twin had one)

The deadline tests did not pin the 60s slack: the 'expired' fixture derived from the constant itself and the 'inside slack' fixture used a hardcoded 1s, so DEADLINE_SLACK could be set to anything and both stayed green

Instant::now() + Duration::from_secs((exp - now).max(0)) has two panic paths on a runtime value (i64 subtraction overflow in debug; Instant+Duration overflow) reachable via an app-supplied IdentityResolver::access_token_exp with no documented bounds

Clock-source mismatch: registry deadline used std::time::Instant while the stream's sleep_until used tokio::time::Instant, so the 'stream always breaks before the registry reaps it' argument silently depended on nobody using tokio::time::pause()

Instant::now() - DEADLINE_SLACK - 30s in the new unit tests panics on a host with under ~90s uptime (std::time::Instant is CLOCK_MONOTONIC-since-boot; Instant::sub panics on underflow) - a plausible CI-container condition

SyncRegistry::prune_closed and prune_closed_for_user shipped as pub SDK API with ZERO production callers, contradicting the diff's own rationale written in the chat twin for gating them #[cfg(test)] (CODING_GUIDELINES §15)

DEADLINE_SLACK, is_past_deadline, is_reclaimable, both *_locked sweeps, the expires_at field and the handler-side computation were copy-pasted verbatim across the crate boundary into the chat registry, roughly doubling the duplicated surface between two registries that were already near-duplicates

The load-bearing safety argument for reaping a connection was undocumented: the registry holds the SOLE Sender clone, so remove_conn closes the channel and the stream self-terminates. A future second Sender clone would silently turn a sweep into an orphaned zombie stream

remove_conn's pre-existing doc comment was orphaned onto prune_closed_locked by the insertion, leaving remove_conn (the helper owning the two-index invariant) undocumented; the SDK twin got the same insertion right, so the two mirrors diverged

expires_at re-derived (exp - Utc::now()).max(0) 35 lines before secs_remaining computed the identical expression with a second Utc::now() call, producing two divergent deadlines for one concept in two different clocks
register's doc claimed 'the registry's only other reaper is deliver's send-failure prune' - deliver_session_to_users also prunes and unregister is a third release path

pub expires_at was a new REQUIRED public field on the SDK's ClientConn with no Default, no constructor and no #[non_exhaustive], source-breaking every out-of-tree struct literal, and its failure mode was silent (None compiles and fails open)

Connection caps were hardcoded as literals in 5 places across the tests (12 twice in sync_routes.rs, 12 twice in subscribe_test.rs, 24 in the chat test) with no compile-time link to their source of truth

Explicit NEGATIVE: no authorization, owner-scoping or audience-routing weakening. deliver, deliver_session_to_users, refresh, all three Audience arms, the admin short-circuit and the permission snapshot are byte-identical; the sweep is keyed on the authenticated user_id, never client input; no cross-user eviction path exists
Explicit NEGATIVE: HTTP surface genuinely unchanged - no openapi.json, no api-client/types.ts, no aide _docs edits in the diff (verified by git diff --name-only)

Sweep cost bounded and allocation-free on the common path: below both caps register does zero extra work; a filtered collect with a 0 size_hint lower bound never allocates on an empty sweep. Residual: the O(512) global scan runs under the same mutex that serializes event fan-out, microsecond-scale
